clue.text: Old lady keeps plant perhaps in shade

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it

blocks.note: ma is a mother, an old lady in slang
a plant is a spy planted in an organisation, one kind of secret agent

explanation.surface: A mother keeps a potted plant sitting in the shade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks botanical, but here it is a spy, and 'perhaps' flags that a plant is only one kind of agent.
explanation.definitionFit: Magenta is a purplish-red colour, and a shade is simply another word for a colour or hue.

clue.text: Cake females will feed Greek character at home

indicators.note: to feed is to put food into a mouth

blocks.note: mu is the twelfth letter of the Greek alphabet
F is the abbreviation for female, doubled for the plural
someone who is in is at home

explanation.surface: Women feeding cake to a Greek friend who has invited them round.
explanation.walkthrough: The two females go between the Greek letter and the word for 'at home', so they sit in the middle of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A muffin is a small cup-shaped sponge baked in a paper case, so it counts as a type of cake.

clue.text: Move using compass, good to begin with

indicators.note: whatever comes to begin with stands at the front

blocks.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
the compass of something is its range or scope, its ambit

explanation.surface: Instructions for navigating with a compass, with a note that good things come first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Compass' suggests a navigation tool, but it is used in its sense of range or scope; 'to begin with' puts the abbreviation for good at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A gambit is an opening manoeuvre in chess or a calculated action in any contest, which is a move.

clue.text: Organised trek with Rhona touring old country

indicators.note: things that are organised are put into a new arrangement
a tour goes round a place

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters; 'with' simply joins the two words
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A woman called Rhona organising a trek to tour some old country.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of the nine letters wraps round the O for old, which becomes the second O of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: North Korea is a sovereign state on the northern half of the Korean peninsula, so it is a country.

clue.text: This writer’s upset when framed by past friend

indicators.note: in a down clue, to upset something is to turn it upside down
a frame goes around a picture

blocks.note: the setter speaking of themselves: 'this writer is' shortens to I'M
something past happened a while ago

explanation.surface: The setter is upset at being set up by a former friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This writer' is the setter, a convention for I or ME; here it is I'M, turned over and placed inside AGO.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigo is the Spanish word for a pal, borrowed into English informal speech as a synonym for friend.

clue.text: Book vessel shortly leaving America, heading west

indicators.note: a journey westward runs right to left across a map, so the joined pieces are read backwards

blocks.note: sub is short for submarine, a vessel
'in a mo' means shortly, in a moment, with the article dropped

explanation.surface: A ship about to leave America and sail west.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortly' reads like an instruction to cut the vessel, but it is its own piece: 'in a mo', British slang for 'in a moment'.
explanation.definitionFit: An omnibus is a single volume collecting several works by one author, so it is a kind of book.

clue.text: Former Strictly winner denied charge in court

indicators.note: to be denied something is to go without it

blocks.note: former and old both mean from an earlier time
comedian Bill Bailey won the TV dance contest Strictly Come Dancing in 2020
a bill is a charge you are asked to pay

explanation.surface: A former Strictly Come Dancing champion refused bail when charged in court.
explanation.walkthrough: Strictly Come Dancing is the BBC's celebrity ballroom show; the comedian Bill Bailey won it in 2020, and his first name doubles as a charge.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Bailey is the popular name of the Central Criminal Court in London, England's best-known criminal court.

clue.text: Mounting loneliness envelops banker

indicators.note: in a down clue, mounting means climbing, so the letters are read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the four letters in the middle of the word

explanation.surface: A banker's loneliness grows as they climb the career ladder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banker' looks like someone in finance; in crosswords it is often a river, something that has banks.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossword-only sense: a banker is a thing with banks, which any river has, and the Nile is Africa's longest river.

clue.text: Do a hobby developed in infancy

indicators.note: something developed has grown into a new form

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Advice to take up a hobby that was developed back in childhood.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is the first three words; 'developed' says to shuffle them and 'in' joins them to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Babyhood is the earliest period of life, when a person is a baby, which is what infancy names.

clue.text: Embarrassed that woman and husband after records one breaks

indicators.note: something that breaks into a thing splits it open and sits inside

blocks.note: the pronoun for a woman already mentioned
EPs are extended-play records
the Roman numeral for one
H is the standard abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A woman and her husband are embarrassed after breaking one of their records.
explanation.walkthrough: The I goes inside EPS, between P and S, and the H follows at the very end.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheepish describes the awkward, shamefaced look of someone who knows they have done something foolish, much like being embarrassed.

clue.text: Body part seems regularly covered with hair

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals
a covering goes over and round

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters of the word
fur is the hair of an animal

explanation.surface: A part of the body that looks as if it is always covered in hair.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of 'seems' go inside FUR, between its first and second letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The femur is the thigh bone, the longest bone in the human skeleton, and so a part of the body.

clue.text: Popular shop worker mostly accepts student becoming permanent

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all

blocks.note: what is in is fashionable, popular
a deli, short for delicatessen, is a food shop
the worker bee is the crossword's standard worker
L for learner, the letter on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A well-liked shop assistant takes on a student who ends up staying for good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worker' in crosswords is usually a bee or an ant; here BEE loses its last E and takes in L for student.
explanation.definitionFit: Indelible ink or memories cannot be erased or removed, so they are lasting, which is what permanent means.

clue.text: King visits a show I’m in, playing someone from Dublin?

indicators.note: actors playing roles take new forms
a visitor goes inside someone else's house

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A king drops in on a performance the speaker is in.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a definition by example: a Dubliner is only one kind of Irishwoman, and could just as easily be a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Dublin is the capital of Ireland, so a woman born there is one example of a female Irish citizen.

clue.text: Token scratch

blocks.note: a gambling counter used in place of money at a casino
a small nick or mark knocked out of a surface

explanation.walkthrough: Two unrelated senses of the same word, placed side by side with nothing joining them.
explanation.definitionFit: A casino counter standing for money is a token; a small nick in paintwork or crockery is a scratch.

clue.text: Most devoted aunt’s excited to be given box

indicators.note: an excited person is stirred up

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters
a chest is a large box

explanation.surface: An aunt thrilled to be given a present in a box.
explanation.walkthrough: Only 'aunt's' is shuffled; the box word follows unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: Staunch means firmly loyal, as in a staunch supporter, so the superlative means most loyal and committed.

clue.text: Parallels with my family

blocks.note: 'my!' and 'cor!' are both exclamations of surprise
your relations are your family members

explanation.surface: Seeing resemblances between oneself and one's family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' looks like a possessive, but it is the exclamation; cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'blimey'.
explanation.definitionFit: Correlations are connections or correspondences between things, and parallels are likewise similarities that match up.

clue.text: “Judge meets serial killer” reported Mirror

indicators.note: two things that meet end up side by side
a report is what you hear

blocks.note: a ref, or referee, judges a game
Hannibal Lecter is the fictional serial killer in The Silence of the Lambs

explanation.surface: A tabloid headline from the Mirror about a judge meeting a murderer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mirror' is dressed as the British tabloid newspaper, but it is the definition; a lector is a reader in church.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirror bounces back light and images, and anything that does that job is a reflector.

clue.text: Masked son old boy, restored to health, hugs

indicators.note: a hug wraps arms round someone

blocks.note: OB is the abbreviation for an old boy, a former pupil of a school
S is the standard abbreviation for son
someone cured has been made well again

explanation.surface: A masked former pupil, back to health, hugs his son.
explanation.walkthrough: The two outer pieces sit either side of S: the abbreviation first, then the word for healed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something masked is hidden from view, and something obscured is likewise concealed or made hard to see.

clue.text: Want arms to be different for scarecrow

indicators.note: being different means taking another form

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Wishing a scarecrow's outstretched arms could be different.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sits naturally on a scarecrow, which really does have stiff arms, so the anagram hides in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A scarecrow is a figure made of old clothes stuffed with straw, so it is literally a man of straw.

clue.text: Obsessive lepidopterist that one can wind up?

blocks.note: a lepidopterist studies butterflies and moths; an obsessive fan is a nut
a nut with two flat wings that is turned by hand onto a bolt

explanation.surface: An obsessive butterfly collector who is easy to tease.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a whimsical invented reading; the question mark covers it, and 'wind up' shifts from teasing someone to screwing something down.
explanation.definitionFit: A butterfly nut, also called a wing nut, has two flat lugs so fingers can twist it tight without a spanner.

clue.text: Only Macron to appear gutted and glum

indicators.note: a gutted fish has had its insides removed

blocks.note: the sole survivor is the only one
first and last letters of the French president's surname

explanation.surface: President Macron alone looks devastated and downcast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gutted' is British slang for bitterly disappointed, which suits the surface; in the wordplay it means emptied out.
explanation.definitionFit: Solemn means grave and unsmiling, close in mood to glum, which describes a gloomy, serious face.

clue.text: Position figures on plinths with no end of care

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter
having no something means going without it

blocks.note: statues are figures that stand on pedestals
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Positioning figures on their plinths carelessly.
explanation.walkthrough: STATUES loses its only E to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Your status is your rank or standing in society or an organisation, which is your position.

clue.text: River conceals large shellfish

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide something within

blocks.note: the Cam is the river that flows through Cambridge
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A river hiding a big shellfish in its mud.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cam is the crossword's favourite river, the one that flows through Cambridge; the L sits after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A clam is a bivalve mollusc with a hinged shell, one of the many creatures called shellfish.

clue.text: Describing Ruby, occasionally resorted to coarse language

indicators.note: read as re-sorted, sorted again into a different order
to describe a circle is to draw round it

blocks.note: first and third letters of the name
anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: An account of a woman named Ruby who now and then swore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resorted to' looks like one phrase meaning 'turned to', but split it: 'resorted' is re-sorted and 'to' is fodder. 'Describing' in geometry means drawing round.
explanation.definitionFit: Serbo-Croat is the South Slavic tongue spoken in Serbia, Croatia, Bosnia and Montenegro, so it is a language.

clue.text: Mark of tailless creature

indicators.note: an animal without its tail has lost its end

blocks.note: a black-and-white burrowing mammal of British woodland, one possible creature

explanation.surface: The mark left by an animal that has lost its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creature' could be almost any animal, so the definition and length do the work: a five-letter mark plus one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A badge is an emblem or token worn to show rank or membership, a distinguishing mark in that sense.

clue.text: Advertise type of pastry

blocks.note: to praise a product extravagantly in publicity, to hype it
the light layered pastry made by folding butter into dough

explanation.walkthrough: The verb sense is dated but still used, as in a 'puff piece' of flattering publicity.
explanation.definitionFit: Promoting something with exaggerated praise is puffing it; puff pastry is the flaky kind used for vol-au-vents.

clue.text: Horse Oliver maybe welcomes being put on again

definitions.note: a phrase describing the state rather than a single adjective, but it swaps in as a past participle

blocks.note: a mount is a horse you ride
Oliver Reed was an English film actor; 'maybe' marks him as one Reed among many

explanation.surface: The actor Oliver Reed greets a horse he is putting back on show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oliver' is a first name standing for a surname: Oliver Reed, the hell-raising star of Gladiator and Oliver!
explanation.definitionFit: Remounted describes a picture or gem fixed on a new mount, or a play staged again, both put on again.

clue.text: Just time for item in sports programme

blocks.note: even-handed and just both mean fair
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Only just enough time to fit something into a sports day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just' pretends to mean 'barely'; it is the adjective meaning fair.
explanation.definitionFit: An athletics meeting or Olympic schedule lists its races and contests as events, each one an item on the programme.

clue.text: Cross over marshland, turning back having sunk

indicators.note: one thing laid over another covers it
turning back means going the opposite way, so the combined letters are read right to left

blocks.note: a rood is a cross or crucifix, especially one in a church
a fen is low marshy land, as in the Fens of eastern England

explanation.surface: Crossing a marsh, turning back after getting stuck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' here means lying over and round the marsh word, not across it; a rood is the large crucifix above a church's chancel screen.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone done for is ruined or beyond saving, and 'sunk' is informal for exactly that doomed state.

clue.text: Unfolds sexy item Andy repeatedly discovered sweetheart’s opening

indicators.note: discovered means uncovered, with the outer covering stripped, done again for each of the three words before it

blocks.note: the word with its first and last letters removed
the word with its first and last letters removed
the name with its first and last letters removed
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A sexy couple uncovered: Andy and his sweetheart, caught in the act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Item' is a couple here in the surface, but in the wordplay it is just a word to strip, like its neighbours.
explanation.definitionFit: When something unfolds, such as a map or a wing, it opens out and stretches, which is what extends means.
